sentences.text: Parahelicoprion is a genus containing two species, one from Russia and another from Bolivia, belonging to the family Helicoprionidae within the order Eugeneodontiformes.

Both species share tooth crowns with long, backwards-sweeping recessed lower sections and curved denticles along their edges, featuring uniquely rounded and blunt upper tips unlike the pointed tips of many related edestoids.
The holotype of Parahelicoprion clerci, prepared and assembled by Karpinsky in 1916, measures 25 cm in profile and includes six articulated tooth crowns plus a smaller fragment.
Parahelicoprion mariosuarezi preserves a denticle-bearing parasymphyseal tooth near the midline of the mouth, a type not found in P. clerci.
The upper tips of Parahelicoprion tooth crowns are uniquely rounded and blunt, unlike the pointed tips of many related edestoids.
The rear edges of the frontmost tooth crowns form sharp, non-serrated cutting blades, while in the rear tooth crowns, both the front and rear edges are blade-like.
The rear portion of the whorl in Parahelicoprion mariosuarezi is described as fused.
The genus Parahelicoprion was formally described by Karpinsky in 1924.
Parahelicoprion mariosuarezi was described by Merino-Rodo and Janvier in 1986.
The type specimen of P. clerci was found in the Ural Mountains of Russia in Artinskian strata.
The holotype of P. clerci consists of tooth fragments that were damaged by mining and broken into pieces.
Like other family members, the teeth of Parahelicoprion angle forward in the mouth.
Parahelicoprion teeth increase significantly in size toward the rear of the whorl, and those farthest forward are rounder and more asymmetrical than the nearly symmetrical rear teeth.
Parahelicoprion was a carnivore that lived in marine environments, and it has been suggested that it was the apex predator of its ecosystem, with its serrated tooth whorl adapted for cutting prey.
It is hypothesized that members of the Helicoprionidae were molluscivorous, feeding primarily on ammonoid and coleoid cephalopods.
Due to incomplete fossils, estimates of Parahelicoprion's size and ecology are speculative, though it is assumed to have been large, predatory, and potentially pelagic.

Karpinsky suggested Parahelicoprion clerci was very large to accommodate its significantly larger tooth crowns compared to Helicoprion, while Richard Ellis estimated it was at least 100 feet long, unless it had a gigantic head or oversized teeth, though non-academic sources suggest lengths of 11-13 meters that are not supported by scientific literature.
The type species of the genus Parahelicoprion is Helicoprion clerci.
The family Helicoprionidae is defined by possessing tooth whorls with forward-angled, blade-like tooth crowns and often completely fused tooth roots.
Parahelicoprion lived during the Early Permian.

The latest known occurrence of Parahelicoprion is the Artinskian stage of the Permian, and it is assumed to have gone extinct by the end of the Cisuralian, having lived between 298.9 and 293.52 million years ago during the Asselian stage.
Authors have suggested P. mariosuarezi had a short tooth whorl at the tip of elongated jaws, but acknowledged the material is too fragmentary for confident comparison.
It is debated whether crushing teeth similar to Campodus or Orodus were present in Parahelicoprion, as no other teeth are confidently associated with the species.
Estimates of Parahelicoprion's total body size are controversial despite its large tooth crowns.
Karpinsky suggested that the extinction of Uralian edestoids like Parahelicoprion was caused by the disappearance of the seaway connecting the Arctic and Tethys oceans.
